extracted.subtask_description: A student case study analyzing Domino’s 2009 social-media crisis: documents the timeline, evaluates Domino’s strategies (inside-out then outside-in), and provides recommendations for social-media crisis management and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic organizational communication
rubrics_metrics.description: “Strategic organizational communication involves the ability to analyze a situation, select appropriate communication strategies, and enact those strategies effectively” (Conrad, 1994).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation must occur at the proper time to have a strong impact and resolve crises; organizations must adopt appropriate strategies when in crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inside-out perspective / initial internal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an inside-out perspective to focus on internal communication and avoid alerting the public (Domino’s initially tried to minimize public attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inside-out can include communicating with employees, taking internal corrective actions, and attempting to prevent wider attention; the case notes this approach can fail in the age of social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside-in perspective / stakeholder-focused response
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an outside-in perspective: take environmental conditions into account and build long-term relationships by identifying stakeholder interests and needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves using channels stakeholders use, addressing their concerns publicly, and tailoring messages to stakeholder expectations (Domino’s later used this perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — act quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond quickly to emerging crises (Domino’s discovered the need to act quickly after the video spread to >1 million views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay or initial non-response can magnify reputational damage; providing the right information at the right time is a key competence and reputation driver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same social channels your audience uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage on the social media channels where the crisis is occurring (e.g., Domino’s posted a video on YouTube and created a Twitter account @dpzinfo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the same channels helps minimize impact, allows direct response to commenters, and shows the organization is listening to the online community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, apology, and spokesperson visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly acknowledge the incident, apologize, and use credible spokespeople (Domino’s posted a video with its president apologizing and thanking the online community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sincere apology and visible leadership can be more effective than silence; thanking those who alerted the company signals responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive internal/corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Take visible corrective measures (Domino’s identified and fired the employees, called the local health department, and involved police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrable corrective actions help show accountability and can mitigate reputational harm when communicated appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media relations and information control
rubrics_metrics.description: Use media-relations tactics to provide official information (e.g., post official videos, coordinate messaging across channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing the right information at the right time stabilizes reputation; coordinate internal and external messaging to avoid mixed signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-existing crisis/social-media plan and preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a developed social-media/crisis plan ready before crises occur (Domino’s had a plan but it was not developed enough for this event).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans should be sufficiently detailed to handle unexpected or viral incidents; failure to plan is a common, avoidable mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and evaluate response effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure effectiveness of strategies using social-media metrics (Domino’s evaluated by number of video views and viewers’ comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare reach and sentiment of official responses versus offending content; large gaps indicate weaknesses in implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to adapt strategy when initial approach fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate initial responses and change strategy if ineffective (Domino’s switched from minimizing attention to actively using social media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations should not rigidly stick to a failed approach; rapid evaluation and pivoting are crucial in dynamic social-media crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to the public and understand audience concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with and listen to stakeholders’ concerns to understand audience expectations (the case emphasizes listening to public concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listening supports relationship-building and informs appropriate messaging and channels; Seeger (2006) and others cite this as best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid minimizing or ignoring social media attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume non-response will diminish attention; ignoring social media can increase damage (Domino’s initial non-response made the crisis worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional minimization strategies may be ineffective with newer audiences who rely on social platforms for news and mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation foundations: service quality and organizational concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that reputation is based on service quality and organizational concern for issues (Domino’s view of reputation drivers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis responses should reinforce underlying reputation drivers (quality, values) rather than only addressing the immediate incident.
